title: Sonoma County
description: Napa's larger, more varied neighbour: cool coastal Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and old-vine Zinfandel.
L: From the Pacific to the Mayacamas

Sonoma County lies west of Napa, between the Pacific Ocean and the Mayacamas Mountains, about 80 km north of San Francisco. It has about 24,000 hectares of vines, more than Napa, spread over a much more varied landscape: coast, valleys and hills. It has 19 AVAs.
Larger and more varied than Napa

Sonoma's climate ranges from cool and foggy on the coast to warm inland. The cold Pacific creates fog that flows inland through gaps in the coastal hills, especially the Petaluma Gap, cooling valleys like the Russian River. Inland valleys, like Alexander Valley and Dry Creek, are much warmer.
A gap in the hills that lets cool ocean air in
It funnels wind and fog inland.

Russian settlers planted vines at Fort Ross on the coast in 1812. Agoston Haraszthy, a Hungarian, founded Buena Vista winery in 1857, California's oldest commercial winery, and brought many European vine cuttings. Italian immigrants later planted Zinfandel. Sonoma is known for family wineries and a relaxed, rural feel.
Sonoma County has fewer vineyards than Napa.
Not true. Sonoma has more vineyard area than Napa.
Sonoma is larger and more varied than Napa
Ocean fog cools the coast; inland valleys are warm
Buena Vista, from 1857, is California's oldest commercial winery

Chardonnay is Sonoma's most planted grape, and Pinot Noir is close behind. Both thrive in the cool, foggy areas near the coast: the Russian River Valley, Sonoma Coast and Carneros. The wines are fresh, with red fruit and citrus, balanced by acidity.
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in cool areas

In warmer inland valleys, Cabernet Sauvignon thrives in Alexander Valley, giving soft, ripe wines. Zinfandel, often from old vines, thrives in Dry Creek Valley and Sonoma Valley, giving ripe, spicy, bramble wines. Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot and Syrah also grow.
Match each AVA to its grape.
Old-vine Zinfandel from Dry Creek Valley, some over 100 years old, shows the grape at its most complex.
Which is Sonoma's most planted grape?
Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir close behind.
Chardonnay and Pinot Noir thrive in cool coastal areas
Cabernet grows in Alexander Valley; Zinfandel in Dry Creek
Sonoma has a grape for every climate

The Russian River Valley is one of California's coolest areas, thanks to morning fog that can last until noon. Goldridge, a fine sandy loam soil, drains well. Its Pinot Noir is ripe yet fresh, with red cherry, raspberry and spice; its Chardonnay rich with citrus and acidity. Producers include Williams Selyem, Rochioli and Kistler.

The Sonoma Coast AVA is large; its truest coastal areas, near the Pacific, like the Fort Ross-Seaview AVA, sit above the fog line at 300 to 550 m, on ridges. They give lean, high-acid Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, among California's most elegant. The West Sonoma Coast AVA, created in 2022, defines the truly coastal zone.
Above the fog line, on ridges
What makes the Russian River Valley so cool?
Morning fog that can last until noon
Ocean fog flows up the river valley.

Fog slows ripening by blocking morning sun and keeping temperatures low, then lifts to let afternoon sun ripen the grapes. This long, slow season builds flavour while keeping acidity. It's why Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, which need cool conditions, do so well here.
Which are Sonoma's cool coastal AVAs?
Alexander Valley is warm and inland.
The Russian River Valley is cooled by long morning fog
True coastal Sonoma sits on ridges above the fog
Slow ripening gives fresh Pinot Noir and Chardonnay
Reading Sonoma and eating with it

Labels show winery, grape, AVA and vintage. Sonoma County is the broadest appellation; Russian River Valley, Dry Creek Valley or Alexander Valley are more specific. Single-vineyard names, like Rochioli or Bacigalupi, are common. US rules apply: 75% grape, 85% AVA, 95% vintage.

Russian River Pinot Noir suits salmon, duck, mushrooms and roast chicken. Chardonnay suits Dungeness crab, a local favourite, and lobster. Dry Creek Zinfandel suits barbecue, burgers and spicy sausages. Alexander Valley Cabernet suits steak. Serve Pinot at 14 to 16 degrees, Zinfandel at 16 to 17.
Pinot with salmon, Zinfandel with barbecue
